one_liner: Portable MASM v6-compatible x86/x64 assembler in C; forum timings put it modestly ahead of ml.exe on assembly time.
what_it_does: JWasm assembles MASM-syntax sources (16-bit, 32-bit and 64-bit x86) and writes OMF, COFF, ELF32/ELF64, flat BIN, DOS MZ or PE output directly, so Masm code builds on Linux, FreeBSD, DOS, OS/2 and Windows without Microsoft's tools. It is a command-line replacement for ml/ml64 that accepts most ml options and the MASM macro language. Unlike ml, it never launches a linker.
how_it_is_fast: FASTPASS stores preprocessed source lines in memory during pass one, starting at the first instruction or data item, and replays only those lines in later passes. Large leading include files of equates and types (windows.inc from Masm32 or WinInc) are therefore scanned once, not once per pass. Symbols live in chained hash tables (hashpjw; 8009 global and 127 local buckets, the local table added in v1.95 because the earlier linked list was too slow with many local labels). FASTMEM is a bump allocator over 512 kB mmap/VirtualAlloc chunks that frees nothing until exit, and v2.03 cut the average number of passes.
when_to_use: Building existing MASM-syntax code (Masm32, WinInc, DOS or OS/2 projects) on Linux or in CI without ml.exe, with direct ELF, COFF, OMF, PE, MZ or BIN output.
Large sources that pull in big header files of equates and structures, where FASTPASS avoids rescanning them in every pass.
Sources with huge data arrays: the manual notes Masm is very slow on them and can deadlock with COFF output.
Targets or hosts outside Microsoft's toolchain: 16-bit DOS (a reduced build runs on an 8088), OS/2, or a small dependency-free C assembler to vendor.
when_not_to_use: AVX2, FMA, AVX-512 or BMI code: the opcode tables (src/H/instravx.h, src/H/instruct.h) carry AVX entries such as vaddpd, vpaddd and vbroadcastss but no vpbroadcastd, vpermq, vpgatherdd, vpsllvd, vfmadd*, kmovw, andn or pdep.
When assembly speed is the point: in the same masm32-forum timings Asmc was faster (1200 ms vs 1480 ms on a 21,000-line source; 3901 ms vs 4997 ms building m32lib).
Code that depends on OPTION OLDMACROS, EXPR16 or READONLY, on exact Masm listing output, or on ml options such as -link, -Fe, -Fm, -Sc or -Fr, none of which are implemented.

Licence-sensitive redistribution: files are mixed Sybase Open Watcom Public License 1.0 and public domain, there is no root licence file, and the manual may only be redistributed free of charge (relicensing request #20 unanswered).
Projects written for NASM or GNU as syntax: JWasm only speaks MASM syntax.

integration.form: built tool (standalone command-line executable from C sources; MsvcDll.mak and OWWinDll.mak build a Windows DLL)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (GccUnix.mak uses gcc -std=gnu99 -O2; makefiles also for Clang, MSVC, Open Watcom, Intel C, Pelles C, TCC, PCC and BCC); GCC 15's default C23 mode breaks the build ('bool' typedef, old-style function pointers, open issue #52), so keep -std=gnu99
integration.platforms: hosts: Windows, Linux, FreeBSD, DOS (16- and 32-bit), OS/2; targets: x86 16/32-bit and x86-64 (ELF64, Win64 COFF/PE)
integration.thread_safety: Not reentrant: symbol hash tables and module state are static globals (src/symbols.c), so run one assembly per process.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — accepts MASM v6 (and most v8) syntax and the common ml command-line options, but never invokes a linker, ignores PAGE/TITLE/SUBTITLE, and lacks OPTION OLDMACROS/EXPR16/READONLY and options -AT, -Sp, -Ss, -St, -H and -Ta

gotchas: The speed claim is the 2009 sourceforge line 'Since v1.9, JWasm is faster than Masm.' with no numbers. All timings are masm32/masmforum posts seen only as WebSearch snippets (forum hosts unreachable here), measured on posters' own machines. They point both ways: a 2010 JWasm build regressed to about 2,700 ms vs ml's 800 ms on a 12,000-line source, and a 2012 post claimed MASM was about 3x faster on some code (unconfirmed in the thread).
No AVX2, FMA, AVX-512 or BMI mnemonics in the opcode tables; History.txt through v2.21 never mentions them.

Open output-correctness issues: non-zero RELA section contents with pre-2.37 binutils linkers (#12, #57), an internal error in coff.c(1490) (#56) and LEA moffs16 handling (#22). The v2.21 changelog fixes wrong ELF64 addends with explicit addends and per-pass code-buffer leaks for non-OMF formats.
ELF output now defaults to position-independent code (-pic1) in v2.21, which can change code generated from the same source compared with v2.20.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the MASM-compatible siblings, Asmc posted faster forum timings and UASM (HJWasm) was faster on some sources and slower on others. Pick JWasm for the conservative upstream line with a long changelog of Masm-compatibility fixes, DOS and OS/2 hosts, and a C99 code base that builds with almost any compiler. Look at the forks when you need newer instruction sets or maximum assembly speed.
verified_claims_summary: There is no reproducible benchmark. JWasm's own 2009 sourceforge page says only that it has been faster than Masm since v1.9. The numbers come from one forum poster's machine via search snippets: JWasm 1480 ms vs MASM 6.15 and 10.0 at 1800 ms on a 21,000-line source (about 1.2x). Other snippets give 5.5 s vs 6.9 s for ML 6.15 on a 28k-line library and 4997 ms vs 16356 ms for ML 10.0 building m32lib (about 1.25x and 3.3x, derived from snippet data). No hardware, JWasm version or flags are given.
status_note: Actively maintained (v2.20 released 01.12.2025, v2.21 in progress, last commit 2026-06-30, 11 open issues) and small enough to vendor, but the licensing is mixed per file and the speed advantage rests on 2009-era claims and forum anecdotes.
